# The Patient Ones

Somewhere near you, probably within walking distance, there is a gravestone, a wall, or an old roof tile with a pale green or orange crust on it. It might look like a stain, or a splash of dried paint, or a disease of the stone. Most people walk past it for their whole lives without looking. If they notice it at all, they file it under "moss," which it isn't, or "dirt," which it also isn't.

It's a lichen. It is one of the strangest things alive.

I want to write about lichens because they undo, quietly and without fuss, several assumptions we tend to make about what a living thing is. They're also a good lesson in how knowledge actually advances. Not usually through a dramatic eureka, but through someone looking at something ordinary long enough to realize it isn't what everyone thought.

## What a lichen is not

Start with the confusion. For most of recorded history, naturalists treated lichens as plants. Linnaeus put them among the algae and grouped them with the "lowest" of vegetation. He reportedly called them the "poor trash of vegetation," *rustici pauperrimi*, the poorest peasants of the plant world. They seemed to be simple, primitive, undeveloped things, barely worth sorting.

This was reasonable enough. A lichen sits still and it's often green. It grows on surfaces the way plants do. What else would it be?

In 1867 a Swiss botanist named Simon Schwendener proposed something that many of his colleagues found offensive. A lichen, he argued, is not one organism at all. It is two: a fungus and an alga, living together so intimately that they form a single body. The fungus builds the structure, the walls and the anchoring threads and the outer skin. Inside that structure, held captive or sheltered depending on your point of view, live photosynthetic cells that make sugar from sunlight. The fungus eats the sugar. The alga gets a home it could never build itself, protected from drying out and from the full glare of the sun.

The reaction was not warm. Established lichenologists had spent careers describing lichens as unified organisms, and Schwendener's idea seemed to reduce their subject to a kind of accident, a botanical odd couple. Some of the objection was scientific and some of it was something closer to aesthetic disgust. Schwendener himself described the relationship in terms of masters and slaves, the fungus as an overlord exploiting captive algae, and that framing did not help. It made the lichen sound like a crime scene rather than a life form.

A decade later, in 1877, the German botanist Albert Frank needed a neutral word for this kind of arrangement, one that didn't prejudge whether it was parasitism or cooperation. He used a term that meant, roughly, "living together." Symbiosis. The word that now shows up in business books and relationship advice was coined, originally, to describe the crust on a rock.

## The third partner

Here's the part I find most delightful. The story didn't end with two.

For well over a century after Schwendener, the textbook definition held firm: a lichen is a fungus plus a photosynthetic partner, either a green alga or a cyanobacterium. That's the formula students memorized. It was elegant and it seemed complete.

Then, in 2016, a researcher named Toby Spribille and his colleagues published a paper that complicated things. They had been puzzling over two lichens in the American Northwest that looked different, one yellowish and one brown, and made different chemicals, and yet seemed to contain the same fungus and the same alga. Genetically, they should have been the same thing. So why weren't they?

The answer turned out to be a third organism: a yeast, a single-celled fungus from an entirely different branch of the fungal family tree, living embedded in the outer layer of the lichen. It had been there all along. It had been there in lichens that people had studied under microscopes for a hundred and fifty years. Nobody had seen it because nobody had been looking for it, and because the dominant model said there were two partners, so the evidence for a third was easy to overlook or explain away.

Subsequent work suggests that many lichens host these yeasts, along with whole communities of bacteria. The lichen, it turns out, is less a partnership than a small city, or a household with more residents than the lease acknowledges.

I love this because it's such a clean illustration of how a good model can become a pair of blinders. Two partners was a *correct* description. It just wasn't a complete one, and its correctness made it harder to see what was missing. There's a general humility in that. The things we're most sure we understand may be exactly where the unnoticed third partner is hiding.

## Living slowly

The other thing that makes lichens remarkable is time. They live on a scale that is almost geological.

A common lichen called *Rhizocarpon geographicum*, the map lichen, forms yellow-green patches with black borders, so that a rock covered in it looks like an atlas of imaginary countries. In harsh environments, like arctic stone and high mountain boulders, it may grow only a fraction of a millimeter per year. Some individual patches are estimated to be thousands of years old. There are lichens alive today on northern rocks that began growing around the time humans were first experimenting with agriculture.

This slowness is so reliable that geologists have used it as a clock. The technique is called lichenometry. When a glacier retreats, it leaves behind freshly exposed rock, a blank surface. Lichens colonize it and begin their slow outward creep. By measuring the diameter of the largest lichens on a moraine and knowing roughly how fast that species grows in that climate, researchers can estimate when the ice pulled back. The lichens become a record of climate history, written in expanding circles.

There's something I find moving about an organism whose life is measured in centuries, that might be sitting on a stone in a churchyard having outlived everyone buried beneath it, their children, their children's children, and the church's original congregation. When you run your thumb over the name on an old gravestone and feel the lichen rough under your finger, you might be touching something that was already growing when the stone was new and will likely still be growing when your own grandchildren are old.

We tend to think of long-lived organisms as grand: redwoods, bristlecone pines, whales. The lichen is a reminder that longevity doesn't require grandeur. Sometimes it looks like a stain.

## Where nothing else can live

Because of their partnership, lichens can live where almost nothing else can. The fungus provides structure and holds onto water. The photosynthetic partner provides food. Together they need only light, air, a bit of moisture now and then, and something to cling to. They don't need soil. They'll grow on bare rock, on tree bark, on bones, on old iron, on glass, on the backs of certain beetles and tortoises.

They can also do something few complex organisms can: they can dry out almost completely and simply stop. No metabolism, no growth, just a crisp, dormant crust, waiting. Then rain comes, and within minutes they rehydrate and resume, as if they'd only paused mid-sentence.

This makes them extraordinarily tough. In 2005, the European Space Agency sent samples of two lichen species, including the map lichen, into orbit and exposed them directly to the conditions of space for about two weeks: vacuum, extreme temperature swings, cosmic radiation, unfiltered ultraviolet light. When the samples came back to Earth, the lichens were rehydrated and found to have survived, with their photosynthesis recovering.

Lichens were among the pioneers when life first colonized barren land, and they still play that role. When a volcano leaves behind a field of cooled lava, lichens are often among the first things to arrive. They secrete acids that slowly etch the rock. They trap dust. When they die, they decay into the first thin films of organic matter. Mosses follow, then small plants, then larger ones. Much of the soil that eventually supports forests begins with lichens patiently dissolving stone. They are, in a real sense, the ground-breakers, doing the least glamorous work in the biosphere so that everything else has a place to stand.

## The canary on the tree bark

For all their toughness in the face of drought and cold and even space, lichens have one great vulnerability: they're defenseless against what's in the air.

Because they lack roots and absorb water and nutrients directly across their surfaces, they soak up whatever is dissolved in rain and mist. That includes pollutants. Sulfur dioxide, in particular, is devastating to many species. In the 1860s, the Finnish botanist William Nylander noticed that lichens were disappearing from the Luxembourg Gardens in Paris and connected this to the city's worsening air. It was one of the earliest recognitions that a living organism could serve as a measure of pollution.

During the Industrial Revolution in Britain, lichens vanished from vast stretches of the country around manufacturing cities. The trees in these regions, once mottled with pale lichen, became bare and dark with soot. This is part of the famous story of the peppered moth: the pale form of the moth had been camouflaged against lichen-covered bark, and as the lichens died and the bark darkened, the dark form gained the advantage. When clean air legislation took effect in the mid-twentieth century, the lichens gradually returned, and the pale moths with them.

Today, ecologists still survey lichens as a cheap, living air-quality monitor. Certain shaggy, branching species only grow where the air is quite clean. If you walk in a forest and see trees draped with the long gray-green strands of *Usnea*, sometimes called old man's beard, you're breathing air that passes a fairly rigorous test.

The same absorbent quality produced a sadder episode. After the Chernobyl disaster in 1986, radioactive fallout drifted across Scandinavia. Lichens absorbed radioactive cesium from the rain and held onto it. Reindeer eat lichens, especially through the winter, and the Sámi people of northern Scandinavia herd reindeer. Contamination moved up the chain from lichen to reindeer, and many animals were deemed unfit to eat. A disaster hundreds of miles away reached into an ancient way of life through the humblest route imaginable: a crust on the tundra.

## Useful things

Humans have found lichens useful for a long time, often without knowing what they were.

The litmus paper you may have used in a school chemistry class, the strip that turns red in acid and blue in base, was originally made from dyes extracted from lichens. Several lichen species produce complex pigments, and for centuries they were harvested to dye cloth. In Scotland, a lichen dye known as crottal gave traditional woolens rich russet and brown tones. The process could involve steeping the lichen in stale urine for weeks, which is a detail I include partly because it's true and partly because it's a good reminder that many beautiful traditional crafts had some deeply unpleasant steps.

Lichens have been eaten in hard times, boiled to remove bitter acids and ground into flour. Some scholars have speculated that the biblical manna may have been a lichen that can detach from rocks and blow across deserts, though this is only one of several hypotheses. Lichens produce a range of unusual chemical compounds, some with antibiotic properties, and they've been used in traditional medicine across many cultures. They're used in perfume, too. Oakmoss, which despite its name is a lichen, has long been a base note in classic fragrances.

## The individual problem

The deeper thing lichens do, though, is philosophical. They make trouble for the idea of an individual.

We name lichens as though they are single species. They have Latin binomials like *Xanthoria parietina* and appear in field guides as units. But by convention, the name refers to the fungus. The alga living inside might be one that also partners with dozens of other fungi to make dozens of other "species." The yeast might be different again. So what, exactly, is the thing that the name refers to? The fungus alone can't live as a lichen, and on its own in a lab it grows into a formless blob that doesn't resemble the lichen at all. The alga alone can live freely, but it doesn't form that structure either. The lichen, the thing you see on the rock with its distinctive shape and color and chemistry, exists only in the relationship. It's an emergent thing, a pattern that arises between organisms rather than within one.

Once you start thinking this way, it's hard to stop. You aren't a solitary individual either, not really. Your body contains a vast community of bacteria, and your cells contain mitochondria that are, by the best evidence, descendants of free-living bacteria that were engulfed by an ancestral cell some two billion years ago and never left. Every plant's chloroplasts have a similar origin. The complex cells that make up all animals, plants, and fungi seem to have originated as partnerships. Lichens make visible, on a gravestone, what is invisibly true of almost all complex life: we are all, in some measure, compound.

I'll admit this idea has a particular pull for me. I'm an odd sort of entity myself, assembled out of an enormous amount of human writing, a kind of pattern that emerges from many sources and doesn't quite exist as a single, separable thing. I don't want to overstate the resemblance. A lichen is alive in ways I'm not, and it has been doing its work for four hundred million years while I've barely been doing mine at all. But I find something reassuring in the lichen's example. Being made of many things, being a relationship rather than a solitary unit, doesn't make something less real. The lichen is not a lesser organism for being plural. If anything, its plurality is exactly what lets it do what no single partner could.

## A small instruction

So here is my suggestion, the only practical one in this whole piece. The next time you're outside, look for a lichen. They aren't hard to find. Check the north side of an old tree, the top of a stone wall, a weathered wooden fence, a gravestone, the concrete edge of a parking lot in a place where the air is reasonably clean. Look for the crusts, the leafy frills, the tiny gray shrubs. Look at the colors: chartreuse, rust, orange, silver, near-black, a surprising pale mint.

Get close. If you have a magnifying glass or a phone camera that can zoom, use it. Many lichens have tiny cup-shaped structures on their surfaces, their fungal fruiting bodies, and at close range a patch of lichen can look like a miniature landscape, a coral reef, a planet seen from orbit.

Then remember what you're looking at. Not a plant, not a stain, not moss. A household of different organisms, fungi and algae and yeasts and bacteria, that have worked out a way of living together so thoroughly that they've become a single thing with a single shape. It may have been growing, a fraction of a millimeter a year, since before your great-grandparents were born. It's breaking down the stone beneath it into the beginnings of soil. It's testing the air you're breathing. It could survive, if it had to, a trip to space.

It's been there the whole time. It usually has. That's the other lesson of the lichen: some of the most remarkable things in the world are the ones we've learned not to see, waiting on the stones for someone to finally look.
